claims.text: The nanoparticles are equiatomic AuCoCuNiPt high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
The initial nanoparticles are smaller than 10 nm.
The initial nanoparticles have an FCC multi-twinned or icosahedral structure.
The nanoparticles were synthesized by pulsed laser deposition at 873 K on a silicon nitride membrane.
Heating above approximately 673 K activates atomic diffusion in the nanoparticles.
Surface-energy minimization drives Au and Cu to segregate to the nanoparticle surface.
Au and Cu are the low-surface-energy elements responsible for the proposed surface enrichment.
Shape transitions toward more spherical particles locally enhance atomic diffusion.
The segregation process is kinetically controlled rather than thermodynamically stabilized by configurational entropy.
Surface segregation produces particle reshaping or coalescence.
Segregated Au and Cu eventually evaporate and thereby compromise chemical and structural stability.
Heating will progressively eliminate the smallest, 2–4 nm particles.
Heating will widen the nanoparticle size distribution.
Au and Cu evaporation will reduce the average particle size.
Increasing temperature will transform elliptical or icosahedral particles into more spherical particles.
High-entropy alloys are theoretically expected to show sluggish diffusion and elevated thermal stability.
The proposed instability occurs primarily above approximately 673 K and depends on particles being sub-10 nm.
Icosahedral and truncated-octahedral morphologies may differ in the onset and extent of segregation and evaporation.
The proposed experiment heats samples from 298 K to 973 K at 1 K/s under vacuum and analyzes them at 473, 673, 773, 873, and 973 K.
Retention of the initial composition, morphology, and size distribution without significant Au/Cu segregation or evaporation would falsify the hypothesis.
